subject: Networking
stem: At which OSI layer is the protocol data unit called a frame?
option_1: Physical layer
option_2: Transport layer
option_3: Data link layer
option_4: Network layer
answer_text: Data link layer
explanation: The data link layer wraps a network-layer packet with a header (MAC addresses) and a trailer (FCS), producing a frame. The network layer's unit is a packet, and the physical layer handles raw bits, so neither is called a frame.
concept: PDUs: bits (L1), frames (L2), packets (L3), segments/datagrams (L4).

subject: Networking
stem: In classful addressing, to which class does 172.16.5.4 belong?
option_1: Class C
option_2: Class A
option_3: Class D
option_4: Class B
answer_text: Class B
explanation: The first octet 172 lies in 128-191, which means the leading bits are 10, so it is Class B. Class C begins at 192 (leading bits 110).

subject: Networking
stem: Which transport and port does DNS normally use for ordinary queries?
option_1: TCP port 443 only
option_2: TCP port 25
option_3: UDP port 67
option_4: UDP port 53 (TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses)
answer_text: UDP port 53 (TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses)
explanation: Most DNS queries are small, so they use UDP 53 for speed; TCP 53 is used for zone transfers and responses that do not fit. UDP 67 belongs to the DHCP/BOOTP server.
concept: DNS: UDP 53 normally, TCP 53 for zone transfers.

subject: Networking
stem: In socket(AF_INET, type, 0), which type selects TCP?
option_1: SOCK_RAW
option_2: SOCK_STREAM
option_3: PF_UNIX
option_4: SOCK_DGRAM
answer_text: SOCK_STREAM
explanation: SOCK_STREAM gives a reliable byte stream (TCP) and SOCK_DGRAM gives datagrams (UDP). PF_UNIX is an address family for local IPC, not a socket type.
concept: SOCK_STREAM = TCP; SOCK_DGRAM = UDP.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the main purpose of the TTL field and the ICMP Time Exceeded message?
option_1: To stop packets circulating forever in routing loops and tell the source when one is discarded
option_2: To limit how long a TCP connection may stay open
option_3: To encrypt the packet after a set number of hops
option_4: To measure link bandwidth
answer_text: To stop packets circulating forever in routing loops and tell the source when one is discarded
explanation: Each router decrements TTL; at zero the packet is dropped and the source is told with Time Exceeded. TTL counts hops, not connection lifetime, so the second option confuses layers.
concept: TTL bounds a packet's lifetime in hops.

subject: Networking
stem: What does a MAC flooding attack do to a switch?
option_1: It changes the switch's own MAC address
option_2: It encrypts frames so the switch cannot read them
option_3: It overloads the switch's routing table with fake IP routes
option_4: It fills the CAM table with bogus MAC addresses so the switch floods frames out of every port like a hub
answer_text: It fills the CAM table with bogus MAC addresses so the switch floods frames out of every port like a hub
explanation: When the CAM table is full, unknown destinations are flooded, so an attacker on any port can sniff traffic. Switches forward on MAC tables, not IP routing tables.
concept: CAM overflow -> fail-open flooding -> sniffing.

subject: Networking
stem: How does DNSSEC defend against cache poisoning?
option_1: It encrypts all DNS queries end to end
option_2: It switches DNS from UDP to TCP
option_3: Authoritative servers sign records and resolvers verify the signatures, rejecting forged data
option_4: It hides the transaction ID from attackers
answer_text: Authoritative servers sign records and resolvers verify the signatures, rejecting forged data
explanation: DNSSEC provides origin authentication and integrity of DNS data with public-key signatures. It does not encrypt queries, which is the job of DNS over TLS or HTTPS.
concept: DNSSEC = signed DNS data, not encrypted DNS.

subject: Networking
stem: Which Snort rule action takes effect only when Snort runs inline as an IPS?
option_1: log
option_2: drop
option_3: alert
option_4: pass
answer_text: drop
explanation: drop (and block, reject) discard packets, which is only possible when Snort sits in the traffic path. alert and log work in passive IDS mode as well.
concept: IDS: alert/log/pass; inline IPS adds drop/block/reject.

subject: Networking
stem: What does a one-time pad need to achieve perfect secrecy?
option_1: A truly random key at least as long as the message, never reused
option_2: A key of 128 bits used for every message
option_3: A secret algorithm known only to the two parties
option_4: A key derived from the user's password
answer_text: A truly random key at least as long as the message, never reused
explanation: Shannon showed perfect secrecy needs |K| >= |M| and fresh keys; reuse leaks m1 XOR m2. A fixed 128-bit key for every message may be computationally secure but is not perfect secrecy.
concept: OTP: random, as long as the message, used once.

subject: Networking
stem: On which hard problem does Diffie-Hellman key agreement rely?
option_1: Finding hash collisions
option_2: The discrete logarithm problem
option_3: Integer factorisation
option_4: The knapsack problem
answer_text: The discrete logarithm problem
explanation: Given g, p and g^a mod p, recovering a should be infeasible for large p. Factorisation is RSA's hard problem.
concept: DH = discrete log; RSA = factoring.

subject: Networking
stem: Why do two hosts with two-way IPsec traffic need two security associations (SAs)?
option_1: SAs expire after one packet
option_2: Each host can store only one SA
option_3: One SA is for AH and the other must be for IKE
option_4: An SA is simplex (one-way), so each direction needs its own
answer_text: An SA is simplex (one-way), so each direction needs its own
explanation: Each SA protects traffic in one direction with its own keys and SPI. IKE has its own separate SA, but that is not why data traffic needs a pair.
concept: SA = one-way; bidirectional traffic needs two.

subject: Networking
stem: How does steganography differ from encryption?
option_1: Steganography hides the existence of a message inside a carrier; encryption makes a visible message unreadable
option_2: Steganography always uses stronger keys
option_3: Encryption hides data inside images
option_4: They are the same technique
answer_text: Steganography hides the existence of a message inside a carrier; encryption makes a visible message unreadable
explanation: A stego image looks normal, while ciphertext is obviously ciphertext. Encryption does not hide data in images; that description belongs to steganography.
concept: Stego conceals presence; encryption conceals content.

subject: Networking
stem: A packet travels host S -> R1 -> R2 -> R3 -> server. Compare the frame R2 sends to R3 with the frame R1 sent to R2. What has changed?
option_1: Nothing changes, because frames are forwarded unmodified end to end
option_2: The TCP source and destination ports are rewritten at each hop
option_3: Only the source and destination MAC addresses; the IP addresses and ports are unchanged
option_4: The source IP is rewritten to R2's address and the destination IP to R3's
answer_text: Only the source and destination MAC addresses; the IP addresses and ports are unchanged
explanation: Each router strips the incoming frame and builds a new one with its own MAC as source and the next hop's MAC as destination, while leaving the IP header addresses intact. Rewriting IP addresses per hop would make end-to-end routing impossible (NAT is a special case, not normal forwarding).
concept: Per hop: MAC addresses change; end-to-end IP addresses and ports do not.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the network address of the host 10.45.77.200/20?
explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0. In the third octet, 77 AND 240 = 64, so the network is 10.45.64.0. 10.45.77.0 wrongly assumes a /24 boundary; 10.45.80.0 is the next block, not the one containing .77.
concept: Network ID = IP AND mask; the interesting octet decides the answer.
source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 19

subject: Networking
stem: A page has one HTML file and 5 images. Using non-persistent HTTP/1.0 with serial requests and ignoring transmission time, how many RTTs elapse before everything arrives?
option_1: 10 RTTs
option_2: 6 RTTs
option_3: 12 RTTs
option_4: 7 RTTs
answer_text: 12 RTTs
explanation: Each object needs its own TCP connection (1 RTT) plus the request/response (1 RTT): 6 objects x 2 RTT = 12. 7 RTTs is the persistent-connection figure (1 handshake + 6 requests).
concept: Non-persistent: ~2 RTT per object; persistent: 1 RTT per object after setup.
source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 27

subject: Networking
stem: A TCP segment has sequence number 34,500 and carries 1,460 bytes. If it arrives correctly, what acknowledgement number does the receiver send?
explanation: ACK = sequence number of the first byte + data length = 34,500 + 1,460 = 35,960 (the next byte expected). 35,959 is the last byte received, not the next one expected.
concept: ACK number = last byte received + 1.

subject: Networking
stem: Host S sends a packet with TTL = 3 towards R through routers R1, R2, R3 and R4. Where is it discarded, and who is told?
option_1: At R4, which sends Time Exceeded to S
option_2: At R3, which sends ICMP Time Exceeded to S
option_3: At R, which sends Destination Unreachable to S
option_4: At R2, which sends Time Exceeded to R1
answer_text: At R3, which sends ICMP Time Exceeded to S
explanation: R1 decrements 3 to 2, R2 to 1, and R3 to 0; R3 is not the destination, so it drops the packet and reports to the source. ICMP errors go to the original source, never to the previous router.
concept: The router that decrements TTL to 0 discards and reports to the source.

subject: Networking
stem: An attacker captures a valid authentication token and sends it again an hour later to gain access. Which attack is this?
option_1: Masquerade without capture
option_2: Traffic analysis
option_3: Modification of message
option_4: Replay
answer_text: Replay
explanation: A replay re-sends a captured valid data unit unchanged to produce an unauthorised effect. Modification would alter the contents; here the token is reused exactly as captured.
concept: Replay = capture and retransmit a valid unit.

subject: Networking
stem: A DHCP pool has 120 free addresses. An attacker sends 400 DISCOVER messages per minute with unique MACs. Roughly how long until the pool is exhausted?
option_1: 18 minutes
option_2: 3.3 minutes
option_3: 18 seconds
option_4: 0.3 seconds
answer_text: 18 seconds
explanation: Time = free addresses / rate = 120/400 = 0.3 min = 18 s. Reading 0.3 as seconds (or 18 as minutes) is the unit slip the notes flag in a slide.
concept: Exhaustion time = free addresses / request rate; watch the units.

subject: Networking
stem: An off-path attacker triggers a lookup of a domain it controls and sees transaction ID 3,150. The resolver uses sequential IDs. Which ID should the attacker put in forged replies to the resolver's next query?
option_4: Any random value, since IDs are not checked
explanation: Sequential IDs make the next query's ID predictable (ID + 1), so the attacker races the genuine reply with 3,151. Reusing 3,150 would match the old query, which has already been answered.
concept: Sequential transaction IDs let off-path attackers predict the next ID.

subject: Networking
stem: What does the tcpdump filter 'tcp[13] & 0x12 == 0x02' capture?
option_1: Only initial SYN segments (SYN set, ACK clear)
option_2: Only RST segments
option_3: Any segment with SYN or ACK set
option_4: SYN-ACK segments only
answer_text: Only initial SYN segments (SYN set, ACK clear)
explanation: Byte 13 holds the flags; masking with 0x12 keeps SYN (0x02) and ACK (0x10), and requiring 0x02 means SYN on, ACK off. SYN-ACK would give 0x12 after masking, so it is excluded.
concept: Mask the flags byte, then compare.

subject: Networking
stem: Encrypt the letter 'm' with the additive cipher, key k = 17 (a = 0).
option_1: D
option_2: R
option_3: V
option_4: E
answer_text: D
explanation: 'm' = 12; (12 + 17) mod 26 = 3 = 'D'. 'V' comes from subtracting the key, which is decryption.
concept: C = (P + k) mod 26.

subject: Networking
stem: A 4-stage LFSR has state (z0, z1, z2, z3) = (1, 0, 0, 1). Each tick it outputs z0, shifts left, and sets the new z3 = z0 XOR z1. What are the first 8 output bits?
explanation: Ticks: output 1, new bit 1^0=1 -> (0,0,1,1); output 0, new 0^0=0 -> (0,1,1,0); and so on, giving 10011010. '10010001' uses taps z0 and z3 instead of z0 and z1; '10011001' simply repeats the seed.
concept: Track the full state each tick: output, shift, insert feedback.

subject: Networking
stem: Diffie-Hellman with p = 29, g = 2. Alice picks a = 5, Bob picks b = 11. What shared key do they compute?
explanation: A = 2^5 mod 29 = 3, B = 2^11 mod 29 = 18; K = B^a mod p = 18^5 mod 29 = 15 (and A^b gives the same). 3 and 18 are the public half-keys, not the shared key.
concept: K = B^a mod p = A^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p.
source: Scenario type: Kaufman, Perlman & Speciner, Network Security, ch. 6

subject: Networking
stem: An AH header carries a 96-bit ICV after its 12 fixed bytes. What value goes in the AH Payload Length field?
explanation: Total AH length = 12 + 12 = 24 bytes = 6 32-bit words; the field holds words minus 2 = 4. Writing 6 forgets the minus-2 rule.
concept: AH Payload Length = (AH length in 32-bit words) - 2.

subject: Networking
stem: A file named invoice.jpg begins with bytes 4D 5A 90 00. What should the examiner conclude?
option_1: It is a ZIP archive
option_2: It is a PNG image renamed to .jpg
option_3: It is a corrupted JPEG
option_4: It is a Windows executable disguised with an image extension
answer_text: It is a Windows executable disguised with an image extension
explanation: 4D 5A ('MZ') is the DOS/PE executable signature; a JPEG would start FF D8 FF. A corrupted JPEG would still normally keep its SOI marker.
concept: Extensions can lie; magic numbers do not.

subject: Networking
stem: An attack path has three hops with trust (success) values 0.9, 0.7 and 0.5. What is the path's combined trust score?
explanation: Series hops multiply: 0.9 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.315. 2.1 adds the values, which would exceed 1 and cannot be a probability.
concept: Series: T = T1 x T2 x ... x Tk.

subject: Networking
stem: A public web portal suffers both HTTP floods and SQL injection. Budget allows one new control this quarter. Which choice is best justified?
option_1: Switch port security, because it limits how many hosts can connect
option_2: Doubling uplink bandwidth, because floods then cannot fill the link
option_3: uRPF on the edge router, because it removes all malicious traffic
option_4: A web application firewall with rate limiting, because both attacks live at Layer 7 and need payload-aware inspection
answer_text: A web application firewall with rate limiting, because both attacks live at Layer 7 and need payload-aware inspection
explanation: Both threats are application-layer: floods use valid HTTP requests and SQLi hides in request bodies, so a WAF with request-rate controls addresses both. uRPF only removes some spoofed-source traffic; HTTP floods normally come from real, unspoofed bot addresses over completed TCP connections.
concept: Choose controls at the layer where the attack operates.

subject: Networking
stem: Which control set best protects users of a café Wi-Fi network against Ettercap-style ARP man-in-the-middle attacks?
option_1: Client isolation and DAI with DHCP snooping on the network, plus mandatory HTTPS with HSTS for services
option_2: A longer DHCP lease time and a larger address pool
option_3: Static ARP entries on every customer laptop, entered by staff
option_4: SYN cookies on the access point
answer_text: Client isolation and DAI with DHCP snooping on the network, plus mandatory HTTPS with HSTS for services
explanation: Isolation and DAI stop poisoning at the network, and HTTPS/HSTS keep data safe even if a MitM succeeds. Static ARP on transient customer laptops is unmanageable and leaves the access point's own table open.
concept: Layer the defences: prevent poisoning, and encrypt in case prevention fails.

subject: Networking
stem: For a new secure messaging protocol, which stream-cipher choice is best justified?
option_1: A 64-bit LFSR, because it is fast in hardware
option_2: RC4 with a 256-bit key, since longer keys remove its biases
option_3: ChaCha20 (with Poly1305 authentication), because RC4's biases have led to its prohibition in TLS
option_4: RC4-drop[768] without authentication, since dropped bytes make it unbreakable
answer_text: ChaCha20 (with Poly1305 authentication), because RC4's biases have led to its prohibition in TLS
explanation: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is a modern, well-analysed authenticated design. Longer RC4 keys do not remove its keystream biases, and dropping initial bytes leaves long-term biases and gives no integrity.
concept: Choose current, authenticated primitives over patched legacy ones.

subject: Networking
stem: Which OSI layer is responsible for process-to-process delivery using port numbers?
option_1: Data link layer
option_2: Transport layer
option_3: Network layer
option_4: Session layer
answer_text: Transport layer
explanation: Ports identify the process on a host, and the transport layer (TCP/UDP) uses them for multiplexing and demultiplexing. The network layer only gets a packet from host to host; it has no notion of which application should receive it.
concept: Network layer = host-to-host; transport layer = process-to-process.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the default subnet mask of a Class C network?
explanation: Class C uses three octets for the network ID and one for hosts, so the default mask is /24. /26 is a subnetted Class C mask, not the default.
concept: Default masks: A /8, B /16, C /24.

subject: Networking
stem: Why is FTP described as an out-of-band protocol?
option_1: It needs an e-mail server to deliver the files
option_2: It sends commands over UDP and files over TCP
option_3: It uses a separate control connection (port 21) and data connection (port 20 or dynamic)
option_4: It carries commands and file data on one TCP connection
answer_text: It uses a separate control connection (port 21) and data connection (port 20 or dynamic)
explanation: FTP keeps commands and replies on a persistent control channel and opens data connections per transfer. HTTP, by contrast, is in-band: commands and content share one connection.
concept: FTP: control 21 (persistent), data 20 (per transfer).

subject: Networking
stem: Why does server code call htons(PORT) before bind()?
option_1: To convert a host name into an IP address
option_2: To choose a free ephemeral port
option_3: To convert the 16-bit port from host byte order to network (big-endian) byte order
option_4: To encrypt the port number
answer_text: To convert the 16-bit port from host byte order to network (big-endian) byte order
explanation: Protocol headers use big-endian order, but many CPUs are little-endian, so htons converts the value. Converting names to addresses is a resolver function, not htons.
concept: htons = host-to-network short (16-bit).

subject: Networking
stem: What is the main advance of DHCP over BOOTP?
option_1: DHCP assigns MAC addresses to clients
option_2: DHCP can lease addresses dynamically from a pool for a set time, as well as use static bindings
option_3: DHCP no longer needs relay agents
option_4: DHCP uses TCP instead of UDP
answer_text: DHCP can lease addresses dynamically from a pool for a set time, as well as use static bindings
explanation: BOOTP relies on a static MAC-to-IP table; DHCP adds a pool with lease times and renewal. DHCP still uses UDP 67/68 and still needs relay agents across routers.
concept: DHCP = static + dynamic (leased) allocation.

subject: Networking
stem: Which property of ARP makes ARP spoofing possible?
option_1: ARP runs over TCP, which can be hijacked
option_2: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated, so hosts accept unsolicited replies and overwrite cache entries
option_3: ARP replies are always broadcast
option_4: ARP is encrypted with a weak key
answer_text: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated, so hosts accept unsolicited replies and overwrite cache entries
explanation: Hosts cache any ARP reply, even one they never asked for, with no check of who sent it. ARP is not encrypted at all, and it is carried directly in Ethernet frames rather than over TCP.
concept: No authentication in ARP -> forged IP-to-MAC bindings.

subject: Networking
stem: In a DNS amplification attack, whose address appears as the source of the attacker's small queries?
option_1: The root server's
option_2: The open resolver's
option_3: The victim's
option_4: The attacker's own
answer_text: The victim's
explanation: Spoofing the victim's address makes the reflectors send their large responses to the victim. Using the attacker's own address would send the flood back to the attacker.
concept: Reflection/amplification: spoof the victim as the source.

subject: Networking
stem: What does httprobe do?
option_1: Scans all 65,535 TCP ports on each host
option_2: Crawls every link on a site
option_3: Tests web servers for known CVEs
option_4: Reads domains from standard input and prints the http:// and https:// URLs that respond
answer_text: Reads domains from standard input and prints the http:// and https:// URLs that respond
explanation: httprobe checks whether hosts answer HTTP/HTTPS (ports 80/443 by default, plus custom ones). It does not scan non-HTTP ports or test vulnerabilities.
concept: httprobe = live web-service discovery.

subject: Networking
stem: Which statement correctly contrasts stream and block ciphers?
option_1: A stream cipher uses two keys; a block cipher uses one
option_2: Block ciphers never need padding
option_3: RC4 is a block cipher and AES is a stream cipher
option_4: A stream cipher encrypts one bit or byte at a time with a keystream; a block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks, padding the last one
answer_text: A stream cipher encrypts one bit or byte at a time with a keystream; a block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks, padding the last one
explanation: RC4 and ChaCha20 are stream ciphers; DES (64-bit blocks) and AES (128-bit blocks) are block ciphers that pad the final block. The last option swaps the two families.
concept: Stream = symbol by symbol; block = fixed chunks plus padding.

subject: Networking
stem: On which hard problem does RSA rely?
option_1: Inverting a hash function
option_2: Factoring the modulus n = p x q into its primes
option_3: Solving linear equations over GF(2)
option_4: Computing discrete logarithms mod p
answer_text: Factoring the modulus n = p x q into its primes
explanation: Knowing p and q gives phi(n) and hence d; without them d is out of reach for large n. Linear equations over GF(2) are how LFSRs are broken.
concept: RSA security = hardness of factoring n.

subject: Networking
stem: Which three values identify a security association?
option_1: Source port, destination port and protocol
option_2: Source IP, TTL and SPI
option_3: SPI, destination IP address and security protocol (AH or ESP)
option_4: Encryption key, MAC key and lifetime
answer_text: SPI, destination IP address and security protocol (AH or ESP)
explanation: The receiver uses the SPI in the header, plus destination and protocol, to look up the SA in its SAD. Keys and lifetime are stored in the SA entry; they do not identify it.
concept: SA identifier: (SPI, destination, protocol).

subject: Networking
stem: Which of these is system metadata rather than application metadata?
option_1: The author name inside a Word document
option_2: EXIF GPS coordinates in a photo
option_3: Revision history embedded in a PDF
option_4: A file's modified, accessed and created (MAC) timestamps
answer_text: A file's modified, accessed and created (MAC) timestamps
explanation: The file system maintains timestamps, permissions and ownership; application metadata lives inside the file, such as EXIF or document properties. GPS coordinates are written by the camera into the file itself.
concept: System metadata: file system; application metadata: inside the file.

subject: Networking
stem: Router R2 on a path is compromised. The application payload is protected with TLS. What can the attacker on R2 read from transiting packets?
option_1: Nothing at all, because TLS also encrypts the IP and TCP headers
option_2: Only MAC addresses, because routers never examine IP headers
option_3: Source/destination IP addresses and TCP ports, plus link-layer MACs, but not the plaintext message
option_4: The plaintext message, because routers decrypt traffic at Layer 3
answer_text: Source/destination IP addresses and TCP ports, plus link-layer MACs, but not the plaintext message
explanation: TLS encrypts the application data above TCP, so headers below it (IP addresses, ports) stay readable to any hop. Claiming TLS hides IP and TCP headers is the common mistake; those headers must stay in clear for routing and delivery.
concept: Encryption protects only what is above the layer that applies it.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the directed broadcast address of 172.20.130.17/18?
explanation: A /18 block in the third octet has size 64: blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. 130 falls in 128-191, so the broadcast is 172.20.191.255. 172.20.255.255 would be the broadcast of the whole /16.
concept: Broadcast = network ID with all host bits set to 1.

subject: Networking
stem: The same page (1 HTML + 5 images) is fetched with persistent HTTP/1.1 without pipelining. How many RTTs, ignoring transmission time?
option_1: 6 RTTs
option_2: 12 RTTs
option_3: 7 RTTs
option_4: 2 RTTs
answer_text: 7 RTTs
explanation: One RTT sets up the TCP connection, then each of the 6 objects needs one request/response RTT on the same connection: 1 + 6 = 7. 12 RTTs would mean opening a new connection per object.
concept: Persistent connections pay the handshake once per session.

subject: Networking
stem: An IPv4 packet has total length 1,200 bytes, IP header 20 bytes and a TCP header with options of 32 bytes. The TCP sequence number is 7,000. What is the acknowledgement number for this segment?
explanation: Data = 1,200 - 20 - 32 = 1148 bytes, so ACK = 7,000 + 1148 = 8148. 8,160 assumes a 20-byte TCP header and ignores the 12 bytes of options.
concept: Payload = IP total length - IP header - TCP header.
source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 23

subject: Networking
stem: Traceroute sends a probe with TTL = 4 and receives a Time Exceeded message. What does that reveal?
option_1: That the destination is four hops away and reachable
option_2: The identity (address) of the fourth router on the path
option_3: That the fourth router is congested
option_4: That the destination port is closed
answer_text: The identity (address) of the fourth router on the path
explanation: Each TTL value makes the router at that hop expire the probe and reply, revealing its address. Reaching the destination would instead produce a reply from the host (e.g. Port Unreachable or Echo Reply), not Time Exceeded.
concept: Traceroute maps hops by incrementing TTL: 1, 2, 3, ...

subject: Networking
stem: A manager sends 'ADD user G, ADD user H'. An attacker alters it in transit to 'ADD user I' and the server applies it. Which property is violated, and which attack is it?
option_1: Availability; denial of service
option_2: Confidentiality; release of message contents
option_3: Integrity; modification of message
option_4: Confidentiality; traffic analysis
answer_text: Integrity; modification of message
explanation: The content was changed in transit and accepted as genuine, so integrity is broken by an active modification. Nothing was disclosed, so confidentiality is not the violated property.
concept: Modification attacks violate integrity.

subject: Networking
stem: A server's SYN backlog holds 4,096 half-open connections. A flood arrives at 20,000 SYNs per second. How fast does the backlog fill?
option_1: About 0.205 seconds
option_2: About 30 seconds, the SYN-RECEIVED timeout
option_3: About 4.88 seconds
option_4: About 12.3 seconds
answer_text: About 0.205 seconds
explanation: t = B / R = 4096/20000 = 0.2048 s. The timeout only controls when entries expire; it does not set how fast the queue fills.
concept: Fill time = capacity / arrival rate.

subject: Networking
stem: A resolver randomises both the 16-bit transaction ID and the 16-bit UDP source port. How many combinations must a blind attacker cover?
explanation: Independent 16-bit values multiply: 2^16 x 2^16 = 2^32. Adding them (2^17) is the classic mistake; combinations multiply, not add.
concept: Port randomisation multiplies the guessing space.

subject: Networking
stem: An analyst uses 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' to count connection attempts during a suspected flood. What is wrong?
option_1: It matches nothing because tcpflags is not a valid name
option_2: It counts UDP packets too
option_3: It also matches SYN-ACK replies, so it overcounts; use tcp[13] & 0x12 == 0x02
option_4: It matches only RST packets
answer_text: It also matches SYN-ACK replies, so it overcounts; use tcp[13] & 0x12 == 0x02
explanation: Any segment with the SYN bit set passes, including the server's SYN-ACKs. tcpflags is a valid tcpdump keyword, so the filter does work, just too broadly.
concept: SYN != 0 also catches SYN-ACK.

subject: Networking
stem: Decrypt ciphertext letter 'C' from the additive cipher with key k = 9.
option_1: u
option_2: l
option_3: t
option_4: h
answer_text: t
explanation: 'C' = 2; (2 - 9) mod 26 = 19 = 't'. A negative result must be wrapped by adding 26, not dropped or made positive by sign change.
concept: P = (C - k) mod 26; add 26 to negative values.

subject: Networking
stem: For the same LFSR (new z3 = z0 XOR z1, feedback polynomial x^4 + x + 1), what is the period starting from any non-zero seed?
explanation: x^4 + x + 1 is primitive, so the register cycles through all 15 non-zero states before repeating. 16 would include the all-zero state, which never leaves itself.
concept: Primitive polynomial -> maximal period 2^L - 1.

subject: Networking
stem: A relay sees g = 3, p = 19 and Client 1's half-key A = 7. Brute-forcing exponents from 1 upwards, which private value a does it find?
explanation: Powers of 3 mod 19 run 3, 9, 8, 5, 15, 7, ..., so 3^6 mod 19 = 7 and a = 6. a = 4 gives 5, which is the value used in the corrected lab example.
concept: Tiny primes make the discrete log trivial by brute force.

subject: Networking
stem: In ESP tunnel mode protecting an IPv4 packet, what is the Next Header value in the ESP trailer? And in transport mode carrying TCP?
option_1: 50 in both modes
option_2: 17 in tunnel mode; 6 in transport mode
option_3: 6 in tunnel mode; 4 in transport mode
option_4: 4 in tunnel mode; 6 in transport mode
answer_text: 4 in tunnel mode; 6 in transport mode
explanation: Next Header names what is inside: an entire IPv4 packet (4) in tunnel mode, or a TCP segment (6) in transport mode. 50 is ESP's own protocol number, which appears in the outer IP header.
concept: Next Header: 4 = IPv4 inside; 6 = TCP inside.

subject: Networking
stem: A file named report.docx starts with 50 4B 03 04. Signature analysis should flag it as ...
option_1: a mismatch: it is really a PDF
option_2: a mismatch: it is really a ZIP archive, not a document
option_3: an executable disguised as a document
option_4: consistent: Office Open XML documents are ZIP containers
answer_text: consistent: Office Open XML documents are ZIP containers
explanation: DOCX, XLSX and PPTX are ZIP packages, so 'PK\x03\x04' is expected; a check of the internal [Content_Types].xml would confirm. Flagging it as a mismatch is a classic false positive.
concept: Know container formats before flagging mismatches.

subject: Networking
stem: Two independent attack paths reach the same node with trust values 0.6 and 0.5. What is the combined (parallel) trust?
explanation: Parallel paths combine as an OR: 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.6 x 0.5 = 0.80. 0.30 multiplies, which is the series rule.
concept: Parallel: T = TA + TB - TA x TB.

subject: Networking
stem: You are designing defence in depth for a branch LAN with guest Wi-Fi and a public web app. Which layer-to-control mapping is the most complete and correctly placed?
option_1: L2: DAI, DHCP snooping, port security; L3: ACLs with uRPF; L4: SYN cookies and rate limits; L7: WAF and strict TLS settings
option_2: L2: SYN cookies; L3: DAI; L4: WAF; L7: uRPF
option_3: L1: TLS 1.3; L2: uRPF; L3: HttpOnly cookies; L7: shielded cabling
option_4: L2: WAF; L3: SYN cookies; L4: DHCP snooping; L7: port security
answer_text: L2: DAI, DHCP snooping, port security; L3: ACLs with uRPF; L4: SYN cookies and rate limits; L7: WAF and strict TLS settings
explanation: Each control sits where its attack class lives: switches guard ARP/DHCP/MAC tables, routers filter addresses, hosts protect TCP state, and the web tier inspects HTTP. The other mappings put controls at layers where they cannot see the traffic they claim to filter, such as a WAF at Layer 2.
concept: Defence in depth = the right control at every layer, not one control everywhere.

subject: Networking
stem: You run the edge router for an organisation that owns 203.0.113.0/24. Which ingress/egress filtering design correctly limits spoofing?
option_1: Drop inbound packets whose destination is in 203.0.113.0/24
option_2: Drop inbound packets whose source is in 203.0.113.0/24, and drop outbound packets whose source is NOT in 203.0.113.0/24
option_3: Drop outbound packets whose source IS in 203.0.113.0/24
option_4: Allow everything but log packets with SYN set
answer_text: Drop inbound packets whose source is in 203.0.113.0/24, and drop outbound packets whose source is NOT in 203.0.113.0/24
explanation: Outside traffic should never claim your own prefix as its source, and your own hosts should only send with your prefix. Dropping inbound packets addressed to your own network would block all legitimate traffic.
concept: Ingress: no inside sources from outside; egress: only inside sources leave.

subject: Networking
stem: You must fix a chat client that reuses one RC4 key for all messages. Which redesign is sound?
option_1: Prepend the message number to the plaintext but keep the same key
option_2: Derive a fresh per-message key from the shared secret and a unique counter with a KDF, and use an authenticated cipher such as ChaCha20-Poly1305
option_3: Encrypt each message twice with the same RC4 key
option_4: Discard the first 10 keystream bytes of the same key for each message
answer_text: Derive a fresh per-message key from the shared secret and a unique counter with a KDF, and use an authenticated cipher such as ChaCha20-Poly1305
explanation: Unique keys (or nonces) per message prevent keystream reuse, and authentication adds integrity. Encrypting twice with the same keystream cancels out; discarding the same 10 bytes every time still repeats the rest of the keystream.
concept: Unique key or nonce per message, plus authentication.

subject: Networking
stem: When forwarding a packet, up to which OSI layer does an ordinary router process it?
option_1: Transport layer (Layer 4)
option_2: Network layer (Layer 3)
option_3: Application layer (Layer 7)
option_4: Data link layer (Layer 2) only
answer_text: Network layer (Layer 3)
explanation: A router reads the destination IP address and consults its routing table, which is Layer 3 work; it then re-frames the packet for the next hop. It does not need TCP/UDP ports to forward, so Layer 4 is not part of ordinary forwarding.
concept: Routers are Layer 3 devices; switches Layer 2; hubs and repeaters Layer 1.

subject: Networking
stem: A host sends a packet to 255.255.255.255. Which statement is correct?
option_1: It is a directed broadcast forwarded to every network on the Internet
option_2: It is a multicast address for routing protocols
option_3: It is a limited broadcast delivered to all hosts on the local network and never forwarded by routers
option_4: It is the network address of the local subnet
answer_text: It is a limited broadcast delivered to all hosts on the local network and never forwarded by routers
explanation: All-ones is the limited broadcast; routers contain it within the local segment to avoid broadcast storms. A directed broadcast keeps a real network ID with an all-ones host part, such as 20.255.255.255.
concept: Limited broadcast stays local; directed broadcast targets a remote network.

subject: Networking
stem: Why was MIME introduced for e-mail?
option_1: SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII text, so binary and non-Latin content must be encoded (e.g. Base64)
option_2: SMTP could not carry messages longer than 512 bytes
option_3: To replace POP3 for mailbox retrieval
option_4: To encrypt e-mail end to end
answer_text: SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII text, so binary and non-Latin content must be encoded (e.g. Base64)
explanation: MIME encodes images, audio, documents and other non-ASCII data into 7-bit text and labels it with headers such as Content-Type. It does not encrypt anything; S/MIME and PGP add security.
concept: MIME = encoding bridge from binary to 7-bit ASCII and back.

subject: Networking
stem: How does a CRC differ from a cryptographic hash?
option_1: A CRC prevents an attacker from altering data
option_2: A CRC can correct any single-bit error
option_3: A CRC needs a secret key shared by sender and receiver
option_4: A CRC detects accidental bit errors but gives no protection against deliberate tampering
answer_text: A CRC detects accidental bit errors but gives no protection against deliberate tampering
explanation: CRCs are linear and keyless, so an attacker who modifies data can simply recompute a matching CRC. They detect noise but do not correct it; correcting errors needs other codes.
concept: CRC = error detection for noise, not integrity against attackers.

subject: Networking
stem: What are the three objectives of the CIA triad?
option_1: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
option_2: Control, integrity, accountability
option_3: Confidentiality, identity, authorisation
option_4: Cryptography, inspection, auditing
answer_text: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
explanation: The core triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability; authentication and accountability extend it. Accountability is an extension, not one of the three core objectives.
concept: CIA + authenticity + accountability.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the goal of a DHCP starvation attack?
option_1: Steal the DHCP server's private key
option_2: Redirect DNS queries to a rogue resolver
option_3: Crash the client's network card
option_4: Exhaust the server's address pool so legitimate clients cannot obtain addresses
answer_text: Exhaust the server's address pool so legitimate clients cannot obtain addresses
explanation: The attacker requests leases with many spoofed MACs until the pool is empty, which is a denial of service. Redirecting DNS is the goal of a rogue DHCP server, a different attack that often follows starvation.
concept: Starvation = DoS on the address pool.

subject: Networking
stem: Which is one of the three essential properties of a firewall?
option_1: It must run on the same host as the web server
option_2: It must block all ICMP
option_3: It must decrypt all TLS traffic
option_4: All traffic between inside and outside must pass through it (single choke point)
answer_text: All traffic between inside and outside must pass through it (single choke point)
explanation: The properties are: single choke point, only policy-authorised traffic passes, and the firewall itself is hardened. TLS decryption is an optional feature of some products, not a defining property.
concept: Firewall: choke point, policy enforcement, hardened.

subject: Networking
stem: How does a passive IDS differ from an inline IPS?
option_1: An IPS can only work offline on pcap files
option_2: Both must sit inline
option_3: An IDS drops packets; an IPS only logs
option_4: An IDS watches a copy of traffic and alerts; an IPS sits in the path and can drop packets
answer_text: An IDS watches a copy of traffic and alerts; an IPS sits in the path and can drop packets
explanation: An IDS on a SPAN port adds no risk to production traffic but cannot block, while an inline IPS can block but may drop legitimate traffic on false positives. The second option reverses the roles.
concept: IDS = out-of-band alerting; IPS = inline prevention.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the maximum period of an L-stage LFSR?
option_2: 2L
explanation: The all-zero state maps to itself, so at most 2^L - 1 non-zero states are visited before repeating; a primitive feedback polynomial achieves this. 2L is the number of output bits an attacker needs to break the register.
concept: Max LFSR period = 2^L - 1.

subject: Networking
stem: In RSA encryption, which key does each party use?
option_1: The sender encrypts with the recipient's public key (e, n); the recipient decrypts with the private key (d, n)
option_2: The sender encrypts with its own private key; the recipient decrypts with the sender's public key
option_3: Both use the same shared secret key
option_4: The recipient encrypts with (e, n) and the sender decrypts with (d, n)
answer_text: The sender encrypts with the recipient's public key (e, n); the recipient decrypts with the private key (d, n)
explanation: Anyone can encrypt to the public key, but only the holder of d can decrypt. Using the private key on a message is signing, which provides authenticity rather than confidentiality.
concept: Encrypt with public, decrypt with private; sign with private, verify with public.

subject: Networking
stem: What three actions can a Security Policy Database (SPD) entry specify?
option_1: Encrypt, compress, or fragment
option_2: Tunnel, transport, or NAT
option_3: Discard, bypass IPsec, or apply IPsec
option_4: Accept, reject, or log
answer_text: Discard, bypass IPsec, or apply IPsec
explanation: Every packet is matched against SPD selectors and is dropped, passed in clear, or protected using an SA from the SAD. Tunnel and transport are modes of applying IPsec, not SPD actions.
concept: SPD = policy (what to do); SAD = parameters (how).

subject: Networking
stem: How does an EnCase .E01 image protect integrity?
option_1: Each 32 KB block has its own SHA-256 hash and there is no whole-image hash
option_2: Each data chunk carries a checksum (such as Adler-32 or CRC), and one cryptographic hash covers the whole image
option_3: The image is encrypted with the examiner's password
option_4: Integrity is not protected; only compression is applied
answer_text: Each data chunk carries a checksum (such as Adler-32 or CRC), and one cryptographic hash covers the whole image
explanation: Per-chunk checksums catch localised corruption cheaply, and an MD5/SHA-1 (or SHA-256) of the acquired data verifies the whole image. The claim of a cryptographic hash for every block is the error the notes correct.
concept: E01: per-chunk checksum + whole-image hash.

subject: Networking
stem: A laptop shows a link light, but its address is 169.254.12.7 and no web site loads. Using bottom-up troubleshooting, where is the fault most likely?
option_1: Layer 3 address configuration: the host never received an address from DHCP
option_2: Layer 7: the browser's cache is corrupt
option_3: Layer 4: the web server's port 443 is closed
option_4: Layer 1: the cable is unplugged
answer_text: Layer 3 address configuration: the host never received an address from DHCP
explanation: The link light shows Layer 1 is up, and a 169.254.x.x self-assigned address means automatic configuration failed, so the host has no usable IP setup. Blaming a closed server port skips the lower layer that is already visibly broken.
concept: Troubleshoot bottom-up: link, addressing, ports, application.

subject: Networking
stem: You must split 192.168.10.0/24 into at least 6 equal subnets. What mask results, and how many usable hosts per subnet?
explanation: 2^n >= 6 needs n = 3 borrowed bits, giving /27 with 5 host bits: 32 addresses, 30 usable. /26 only yields 4 subnets, and '32 usable' forgets the network and broadcast addresses.
concept: Borrow n bits: 2^n subnets; remaining h bits: 2^h - 2 hosts.
source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 19

subject: Networking
stem: During iterative DNS resolution of www.shop.example, which machine sends the query to the .example TLD server?
option_1: The authoritative server for shop.example
option_2: The local DNS resolver
option_3: The client's browser
option_4: The root server
answer_text: The local DNS resolver
explanation: In iterative mode the root returns a referral and the local resolver itself follows it to the TLD and then the authoritative server. In recursive mode the root would query onward on the resolver's behalf, which is the tempting confusion.
concept: Iterative = referrals followed by the resolver; recursive = each server asks the next.

subject: Networking
stem: In a three-way handshake the client's SYN has Seq = 9,000 and the server's SYN-ACK has Seq = 15,000. What are Seq and Ack in the client's final ACK?
explanation: SYN consumes one sequence number on each side, so the client continues from 9,001 and acknowledges 15,001. Seq = 9,000 forgets that the SYN itself used up 9,000.
concept: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number; a pure ACK consumes none.

subject: Networking
stem: A router drops an ICMP Destination Unreachable message because its queue is full. What does the router send?
option_1: Nothing: no ICMP error is generated about an ICMP error message
option_2: A new Destination Unreachable to the original sender
option_3: A Source Quench to the previous hop
option_4: A Parameter Problem message to the destination
answer_text: Nothing: no ICMP error is generated about an ICMP error message
explanation: Errors about errors could cascade into storms, so ICMP never reports on ICMP error messages. Source Quench is deprecated and, when it was used, it went to the source host, not the previous hop.
concept: No ICMP error for an ICMP error.

subject: Networking
stem: The manager sends nothing, but an attacker injects 'ADD users G, H, I' claiming to be the manager, and the server obeys. How is this best classified?
option_1: Replay, violating availability
option_2: Passive eavesdropping, violating confidentiality
option_3: Traffic analysis, violating privacy
option_4: Fabrication through masquerade, violating authenticity
answer_text: Fabrication through masquerade, violating authenticity
explanation: No genuine message existed to replay or modify; the attacker created one under a forged identity. Replay requires a captured genuine message, which is absent here.
concept: Fabrication = forged message under a false identity.

subject: Networking
stem: Under a continuous SYN flood that fills the backlog in 0.2 s, an admin cuts the SYN-RECEIVED timeout from 60 s to 10 s. What is the effect?
option_1: Negligible: the queue still refills within 0.2 s, long before any entry times out
option_2: Legitimate clients get guaranteed slots
option_3: The backlog doubles in size
option_4: The attack stops, because entries expire six times faster
answer_text: Negligible: the queue still refills within 0.2 s, long before any entry times out
explanation: A timeout only helps if it is shorter than the fill time; at 10 s it is still 50 times longer than 0.2 s. Stateless defences such as SYN cookies, or upstream filtering, are needed instead.
concept: Timeouts do not beat a flood that refills faster than they expire.

subject: Networking
stem: A 60-byte DNS query produces a 3,000-byte response. If an attacker sends 10 Mbps of spoofed queries through open resolvers, about how much traffic hits the victim?
option_1: 500 Mbps
option_2: 50 Mbps
option_3: 10 Mbps
option_4: 3,000 Mbps
answer_text: 500 Mbps
explanation: Amplification factor = 3,000 / 60 = 50, so 10 Mbps x 50 = 500 Mbps arrives at the victim. 50 Mbps confuses the factor with the result.
concept: Victim load = attacker rate x amplification factor.

subject: Networking
stem: A capture shows segments where tcp[13] == 24 (0x18). Which flags are set?
option_1: RST and PSH
option_2: FIN and ACK
option_3: SYN and ACK
option_4: PSH and ACK
answer_text: PSH and ACK
explanation: Flag values: FIN 0x01, SYN 0x02, RST 0x04, PSH 0x08, ACK 0x10. 0x18 = 0x10 + 0x08. SYN-ACK would be 0x12 = 18.
concept: tcp[13] bits: CWR ECE URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 26?
explanation: 7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1, so 15 is the inverse. 19 is the additive inverse (7 + 19 = 26), not the multiplicative one.

subject: Networking
stem: RC4 KSA with key bytes [3, 1, 4] repeated in T. Starting from j = 0 and the identity S, what are S[0..3] after the i = 0 step?
explanation: j = (0 + S[0] + T[0]) mod 256 = 0 + 0 + 3 = 3, then S[0] and S[3] swap, giving [3, 1, 2, 0, ...]. [0, 1, 2, 3] forgets the swap.
concept: Each KSA step: update j, then swap S[i] and S[j].

subject: Networking
stem: In the lab, g = 3, p = 19, Client 1 sends A = 5 and Client 2 sends B = 11. After brute-forcing Client 1's exponent, what key does the relay compute?
explanation: 3^4 mod 19 = 5, so a = 4; K = 11^4 mod 19 = 11. 18 is the figure in the original lab write-up, which used the wrong exponent 6 (11^6 mod 19 = 1).
concept: Recover a by search, then K = B^a mod p.

subject: Networking
stem: Which IPv4 header field is included in AH's integrity check?
option_1: Header checksum
option_2: Identification
option_3: Fragment offset
option_4: TTL
answer_text: Identification
explanation: Identification is immutable in transit, so AH covers it; TTL, checksum, DSCP/TOS, flags and fragment offset may change en route and are zeroed for the ICV calculation. Including TTL would make every packet fail verification after one hop.
concept: AH zeroes mutable fields: TTL, checksum, TOS, flags, fragment offset.

subject: Networking
stem: Carving finds FF D8 FF starting at offset 0x1000 and the matching FF D9 whose last byte is at offset 0x1A3F. How many bytes is the recovered JPEG?
option_1: 2,623 bytes
option_2: 6,719 bytes
option_3: 2,624 bytes
option_4: 2,622 bytes
answer_text: 2,624 bytes
explanation: Size = last offset - first offset + 1 = 0x1A3F - 0x1000 + 1 = 0xA40 = 2,624 bytes. Leaving out the +1 drops the final footer byte.
concept: Inclusive range length = end - start + 1.

subject: Networking
stem: Path A has hops 0.8 then 0.5; path B is a single hop of 0.7. Both reach node X, and a final hop from X to the goal has trust 0.9. What is the overall trust?
explanation: Path A = 0.8 x 0.5 = 0.4; parallel with 0.7 gives 0.4 + 0.7 - 0.28 = 0.82; then x 0.9 = 0.738. 0.820 forgets the final series hop.
concept: Reduce series paths, combine in parallel, then apply remaining series hops.

subject: Networking
stem: You must carve 192.168.50.0/24 into subnets for 100, 50 and 20 hosts without overlap. Which plan is valid?
explanation: Allocating largest first: a /25 (126 hosts) covers .0-.127, a /26 (62 hosts) fits at .128-.191, and a /27 (30 hosts) at .192-.223, all aligned and disjoint. The second plan places .64/26 inside the /25 already given out; the third gives the 100-host LAN a /26 with only 62 usable addresses.
concept: VLSM: allocate largest blocks first, on aligned boundaries, without overlap.

subject: Networking
stem: A firm needs to block unsolicited inbound connections, allow outbound web, inspect HTTP for malicious URLs and log users by name. Which design best fits?
option_1: An application gateway for every protocol and no packet filter
option_2: A stateful filter at the perimeter plus an authenticating HTTP proxy (application gateway) for outbound web
option_3: A stateless filter alone with rules for ports 80 and 443
option_4: DNSSEC on the internal resolver
answer_text: A stateful filter at the perimeter plus an authenticating HTTP proxy (application gateway) for outbound web
explanation: Stateful filtering handles connection direction efficiently, and the proxy adds URL inspection and user identity for the one protocol that needs it. A gateway for every protocol multiplies maintenance and latency; DNSSEC does not filter traffic.
concept: Combine packet filtering with targeted application gateways.

subject: Networking
stem: The lab relay can read RC4 chat because DH used p = 19. The team moves to a 2,048-bit p but still does not authenticate half-keys. Which assessment is correct?
option_1: The relay can still brute-force 2,048-bit exponents in seconds
option_2: Passive brute-forcing of the discrete log is now infeasible, but an active relay can still substitute half-keys and read everything
option_3: Nothing improves, because DH is broken at any size
option_4: The system is now fully secure against the relay
answer_text: Passive brute-forcing of the discrete log is now infeasible, but an active relay can still substitute half-keys and read everything
explanation: Large p blocks the passive DLP attack, but MitM does not need any discrete log; it needs only the ability to swap unauthenticated values. Both fixes are needed: large groups and authentication.
concept: Large parameters stop passive attacks; authentication stops active ones.

subject: Networking
stem: In practical TCP/IP stacks, where do the OSI session and presentation functions usually end up?
option_1: They are dropped entirely, since modern applications no longer need dialogue control or data formatting
option_2: They are moved into the network interface card firmware, which handles encoding and session state
option_3: They are implemented inside the transport layer, where TCP handles encryption and session checkpoints
option_4: They are absorbed into the application layer (e.g. TLS libraries, cookies, JSON encoding)
answer_text: They are absorbed into the application layer (e.g. TLS libraries, cookies, JSON encoding)
explanation: TCP/IP has no separate Layer 5 or 6; applications and their libraries do encryption, encoding and session tracking themselves. TCP provides a reliable byte stream but no encoding, encryption or session semantics, so placing these functions in the transport layer is wrong.
concept: TCP/IP folds OSI Layers 5-7 into a single application layer.

subject: Networking
stem: NS-2 combines which two languages?
option_1: C for the simulation core and Lua for configuring topologies and traffic
option_2: Java for the simulation core and Python for scripting topologies and events
option_3: C++ for the simulation core and OTcl for scripting topologies and events
option_4: Go for the simulation core and YAML files for describing topologies and events
answer_text: C++ for the simulation core and OTcl for scripting topologies and events
explanation: The event scheduler and protocol code are in C++ for speed, and OTcl scripts build topologies without recompiling. Lua configuration belongs to Snort 3, a different tool in this course.
concept: NS-2: C++ core + OTcl scripts; traces viewed in NAM.

subject: Networking
stem: What defines a traditional (stateless) packet filter?
option_1: It judges each packet in isolation against static header rules, keeping no memory of connections
option_2: It tracks every TCP connection in a state table and admits only packets that match an open session
option_3: It reassembles application payloads and inspects them for malware signatures before forwarding
option_4: It authenticates each user before relaying traffic, acting as a proxy between inside and outside hosts
answer_text: It judges each packet in isolation against static header rules, keeping no memory of connections
explanation: Stateless filters look at addresses, protocol, ports, flags and ICMP type for each packet alone. Connection tables are what make a filter stateful.
concept: Stateless = per-packet; stateful = connection-aware.

subject: Networking
stem: Why is unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle?
option_1: DH is only secure for primes below 1,000, so an attacker can factor larger moduli and recover the shared key
option_2: The generator g must stay secret, and an attacker who learns it can recompute the shared key directly
option_3: The shared key itself is sent in clear during the exchange, so anyone on the path can simply read it
option_4: Nothing proves who sent each half-key, so an attacker can substitute its own and share a key with each side
answer_text: Nothing proves who sent each half-key, so an attacker can substitute its own and share a key with each side
explanation: The exchanged values are public, and without signatures or certificates neither party can tell whose half-key arrived. The shared key itself is never transmitted.
concept: Authenticate half-keys to stop DH MitM.

subject: Networking
stem: Which pairing of attack and mitigation is correct?
option_1: VLAN hopping - upgrade every web service to TLS 1.3
option_2: XML external entity injection - enable SYN cookies on the server
option_3: Ping flood - set the HttpOnly flag on all session cookies
option_4: Session fixation - issue a fresh session ID after login
answer_text: Session fixation - issue a fresh session ID after login
explanation: Session fixation relies on the victim keeping an attacker-known ID, so regenerating the ID at authentication defeats it. SYN cookies defend TCP handshakes and do nothing about malicious XML parsing; the other pairings are similarly mismatched layers.
concept: Match the control to the layer of the attack.

subject: Networking
stem: A sender transmits three 1,000-byte segments with Seq 501, 1,501 and 2,501. The first is lost; the second and third arrive. What ACK does the receiver send?
option_1: 1,501, acknowledging the first segment
option_2: 501 (duplicate ACKs)
option_3: 2,501, acknowledging the second segment
option_4: 3,501, acknowledging all three segments
answer_text: 501 (duplicate ACKs)
explanation: TCP ACKs are cumulative: the receiver still waits for byte 501 and buffers the out-of-order data. 3,501 would acknowledge bytes it has not received contiguously.
concept: Cumulative ACK = next in-order byte expected.

subject: Networking
stem: A SYN flood spoofs the source address of a host that is online and active. Why does this weaken the attack?
option_1: The server detects that the host is active and refuses every SYN that carries its source address
option_2: The real host completes the three-way handshake on the attacker's behalf, opening real connections
option_3: The real host receives an unexpected SYN-ACK and replies with RST, clearing the half-open entry
option_4: Upstream routers recognise the active host and drop all packets claiming to come from its address
answer_text: The real host receives an unexpected SYN-ACK and replies with RST, clearing the half-open entry
explanation: A host that did not send a SYN answers a stray SYN-ACK with RST, freeing the server's memory. That is why attackers use offline addresses or botnets that silently ignore SYN-ACKs.
concept: Live spoofed hosts send RST; floods need silent sources.

subject: Networking
stem: Encrypt 'h' with the affine cipher C = (P x k1 + k2) mod 26, where k1 = 5 and k2 = 8.
option_1: R
option_2: X
option_3: J
option_4: U
answer_text: R
explanation: 'h' = 7; 7 x 5 + 8 = 43, mod 26 = 17 = 'R'. Adding before multiplying gives 'X', which applies the steps in the wrong order.
concept: Affine encryption: multiply by k1, then add k2.
source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Cryptography and Network Security, ch. 3

subject: Networking
stem: Why does AH fail through a NAT router?
option_1: NAT strips the AH header from every packet, so the receiver finds no integrity check value to verify
option_2: AH encrypts the IP header, which the NAT router cannot read in order to rewrite addresses
option_3: NAT routers are configured to drop every packet carrying IP protocol number 51 by default
option_4: NAT rewrites the source IP (and ports with PAT), which AH's ICV covers, so verification fails
answer_text: NAT rewrites the source IP (and ports with PAT), which AH's ICV covers, so verification fails
explanation: AH authenticates immutable header fields including addresses, and NAT must change them. AH does not encrypt anything, so the third option is wrong.
concept: AH and NAT are incompatible.

subject: Networking
stem: Which set of four /24 networks can be summarised by a single /22 route?
explanation: A /22 spans four /24s and must start on a third-octet multiple of 4; 4-7 starts at 4, so 200.1.4.0/22 covers them exactly. 2-5 also has four networks, but 2 is not a multiple of 4, so no single /22 covers them without including 0-1 or 6-7.
concept: Aggregation obeys the same rules as CIDR: power-of-two count and alignment.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the directed broadcast address of the classful network 20.0.0.0?
explanation: 20.0.0.0 is Class A (/8), so the host part is the last 24 bits; setting them all to 1 gives 20.255.255.255. 20.0.0.255 would be correct only for a /24 network.
concept: Directed broadcast = network ID with every host bit set to 1.

subject: Networking
stem: Which two attacks are passive under X.800?
option_1: Modification of messages and denial of service
option_2: Release of message contents and traffic analysis
option_3: Replay of captured messages and masquerade
option_4: Masquerade by an impostor and analysis of the traffic
answer_text: Release of message contents and traffic analysis
explanation: Passive attacks only observe; the active attacks are masquerade, replay, modification and DoS. Masquerade changes system behaviour by impersonation, so it is active.
concept: Passive = observe; active = alter or disrupt.

subject: Networking
stem: Where does BPF filtering happen in a tcpdump capture, and why does it matter?
option_1: In Wireshark, after the whole capture has been saved to a pcap file on disk
option_2: In the kernel, so unmatched packets are discarded before reaching user space
option_3: On the remote router, which forwards only the matching packets to the capture host
option_4: In the NIC firmware only, so the operating system never sees the filter at all
answer_text: In the kernel, so unmatched packets are discarded before reaching user space
explanation: Kernel-level filtering keeps capture fast and light at high traffic rates. Wireshark display filters work after capture, which is a different stage.
concept: BPF = in-kernel capture filter.

subject: Networking
stem: What does IPsec tunnel mode add to a packet?
option_1: A second TCP header, so the original segment is carried inside a new protected connection
option_2: A new outer IP header, so the whole original packet becomes the protected payload
option_3: A TLS record header, so the packet is protected exactly as an HTTPS session would be
option_4: Nothing extra; it reuses the original IP header and protects only the transport payload
answer_text: A new outer IP header, so the whole original packet becomes the protected payload
explanation: Tunnel mode wraps the original datagram in a new IP header between gateways, hiding inner addresses when ESP is used. Transport mode is the one that keeps the original header in front.
concept: Tunnel = new outer header; transport = original header kept.

subject: Networking
stem: A router holds the four /26 subnets of 192.168.1.0/24. A packet arrives for 192.168.1.140. Which subnet entry matches after the bitwise AND?
explanation: 140 = 10001100 and the mask octet 192 = 11000000; the AND is 10000000 = 128, so the match is 192.168.1.128. 192.168.1.140 is a host, and routers store networks, not individual hosts.
concept: Routers AND the destination with each mask and compare with stored network IDs.

subject: Networking
stem: The notes once said Source Quench is sent from an overloaded router back to the previous router R1. What is correct?
option_1: It is sent to the destination host, asking the receiver to slow down
option_2: It is still the standard congestion signal that TCP relies on today
option_3: It is sent to every router on the path so all of them reduce load
option_4: It goes to the original source host, and it is now deprecated
answer_text: It goes to the original source host, and it is now deprecated
explanation: ICMP always reports to the source address of the offending datagram, and Source Quench was deprecated in 2012 because it was ineffective and abusable. Modern congestion control uses loss, delay and ECN, not Source Quench.
concept: ICMP messages report to the source; Source Quench is obsolete.

subject: Networking
stem: A stateless ACL allows 'outside -> 222.22/16, TCP, src port 80, dst port > 1023, ACK set'. An attacker sends such a packet with no prior connection. What happens under stateless and stateful filtering?
option_1: Both allow it, because traffic from source port 80 is trusted as web replies by both filter types
option_2: Stateless allows it; a stateful filter (check-connection) drops it as no matching session exists
option_3: Both drop it, because an inbound ACK-flagged segment is always treated as suspicious by filters
option_4: Stateless drops it because of the ACK flag; a stateful filter allows it as a probable web reply
answer_text: Stateless allows it; a stateful filter (check-connection) drops it as no matching session exists
explanation: The stateless rule matches on header values alone, so a crafted ACK packet passes; a stateful filter checks its connection table first. Port 80 is not trusted in itself; only connection state proves the packet is a reply.
concept: Only connection state distinguishes real replies from crafted ACKs.

subject: Networking
stem: Continue the KSA with key [3, 1, 4]: after the i = 0 step j = 3. What is j after the i = 1 step?
explanation: S[1] is still 1 and T[1] = 1, so j = (3 + 1 + 1) mod 256 = 5; S[1] and S[5] are then swapped. 2 forgets to carry j forward from the previous step.
concept: j accumulates across KSA iterations.

subject: Networking
stem: A JPEG displays normally, but a hex editor shows several kilobytes after the FF D9 footer. What is the most likely explanation?
option_1: LSB steganography in the pixel values, which always enlarges the file past the footer
option_2: A corrupted file header that makes the decoder write padding after the image data
option_3: Normal JPEG compression overhead that encoders routinely place after the footer
option_4: Data appended after the end-of-image marker; viewers stop rendering at FF D9
answer_text: Data appended after the end-of-image marker; viewers stop rendering at FF D9
explanation: Image viewers ignore bytes after EOI, so appended data is invisible on screen but obvious in hex. LSB hiding changes pixel bits within the image data and adds nothing after the footer.
concept: Check for data after the footer.

subject: Networking
stem: You must harden a recursive resolver against off-path cache poisoning. Which combination is the strongest correct design?
option_1: Random 16-bit transaction IDs, random source ports, bailiwick filtering of glue, and DNSSEC validation
option_2: Blocking UDP port 53 at the resolver and allowing only ICMP, so that spoofed DNS replies cannot arrive
option_3: Random transaction IDs only, while caching every glue record received so lookups stay fast
option_4: Sequential transaction IDs with one fixed source port, but a much longer TTL on cached records
answer_text: Random 16-bit transaction IDs, random source ports, bailiwick filtering of glue, and DNSSEC validation
explanation: Randomness expands the guessing space to about 2^32, bailiwick checks stop glue injection, and DNSSEC rejects forged data. Longer TTLs keep a poisoned record alive for longer, so they make the problem worse.
concept: Layered DNS hardening: entropy, bailiwick, signatures.

subject: Networking
stem: Which DNS record type maps an IP address back to a host name?
option_1: MX (mail exchanger) record
option_2: PTR (pointer) record
option_3: NS (name server) record
option_4: A (address) record
answer_text: PTR (pointer) record
explanation: Reverse (inverse) DNS uses PTR records. An A record goes the other way, from name to IPv4 address.
concept: A = name to IPv4; PTR = address to name; MX = mail server; NS = name server.

subject: Networking
stem: Why is a rogue DHCP server so dangerous?
option_1: It can remotely disable the victim's host firewall through a DHCP option
option_2: Its OFFER sets the victim's gateway and DNS server, enabling MITM and pharming
option_3: It always crashes the legitimate DHCP server by exhausting its address pool
option_4: It can permanently change the victim's MAC address through the lease it grants
answer_text: Its OFFER sets the victim's gateway and DNS server, enabling MITM and pharming
explanation: Clients accept the first offer, so a rogue server that answers first controls where traffic and name lookups go. It does not need to crash the real server; it just answers faster.
concept: DHCP spoofing -> malicious gateway/DNS -> MitM.

subject: Networking
stem: Why is a plain LFSR keystream insecure?
option_1: It needs a key longer than the message, exactly like a one-time pad
option_2: Its period is always too short to encrypt any message of useful length
option_3: It cannot be implemented efficiently in hardware, so it is too slow
option_4: Its feedback is linear, so about 2L known bits reveal taps and state
answer_text: Its feedback is linear, so about 2L known bits reveal taps and state
explanation: From 2L consecutive bits an attacker solves linear equations over GF(2) (or runs Berlekamp-Massey) to rebuild the register. Long periods are achievable, so period length is not the flaw.
concept: Linearity, not period, is the LFSR's weakness.

subject: Networking
stem: In the formal model, what is an attack graph?
option_1: The set of failing executions L(M) \ P, i.e. every execution that violates the property
option_2: A network topology diagram showing hosts, links and firewalls between the segments
option_3: The set of executions of the model M that satisfy the stated security property P, i.e. the safe runs
option_4: The list of CVEs reported by a vulnerability scanner for every host in the network
answer_text: The set of failing executions L(M) \ P, i.e. every execution that violates the property
explanation: Given the model's language L(M) and the safe executions P, the attack graph is what remains: all executions that break P. Scanner output lists isolated bugs, which is exactly what attack graphs go beyond.
concept: Attack graph = L(M) minus P.

subject: Networking
stem: In iterative resolution, what does a TLD server normally return for a name it does not hold?
option_1: The final A record of the requested host, fetched on the resolver's behalf
option_2: A complete copy of the root zone so the resolver can restart the lookup itself
option_3: A referral naming the domain's authoritative name server (with glue)
option_4: An error telling the resolver to stop, since the TLD does not hold the name
answer_text: A referral naming the domain's authoritative name server (with glue)
explanation: TLD servers delegate: they point to the domain's authoritative server rather than answering for the host. Only the authoritative server holds the final A record.
concept: Root -> TLD referral -> authoritative answer.

subject: Networking
stem: All traffic to a trading desk is encrypted, yet an observer predicts large trades from bursts of message sizes and timing. What is happening, and what helps?
option_1: Release of message contents; use longer encryption keys
option_2: Masquerade by an impostor; add two-factor authentication
option_3: Traffic analysis; pad and mask message sizes and timing
option_4: Replay of old messages; add sequence numbers to each one
answer_text: Traffic analysis; pad and mask message sizes and timing
explanation: Encryption hides contents but not volume, timing or endpoints; padding and constant-rate traffic hide these patterns. Longer keys strengthen secrecy of contents, which is not what is leaking.
concept: Encryption does not hide metadata; padding does.

subject: Networking
stem: During an nmap -sS scan, port 22 returns RST and port 445 returns nothing after retries. How does nmap report them?
option_1: 22 closed, 445 filtered
option_2: 22 filtered, 445 open
option_3: 22 open, 445 closed
option_4: Both reported as open|filtered
answer_text: 22 closed, 445 filtered
explanation: RST means the host is reachable but nothing listens (closed); silence suggests a firewall dropping probes (filtered). open|filtered is used for scans like UDP or FIN, where silence is ambiguous, not for SYN scans.
concept: SYN scan: SYN-ACK open, RST closed, silence filtered.

subject: Networking
stem: Mallory sits between Alice and Bob in a DH exchange with p = 29, g = 2. Alice's a = 5; Mallory replaces Bob's value with M = g^3 mod p. Which key does Alice end up sharing, and with whom?
option_1: 27, shared with Bob only
option_2: 15, shared with Bob
option_3: 3, shared with nobody at all
option_4: 27, shared with Mallory
answer_text: 27, shared with Mallory
explanation: Alice computes M^a = 8^5 mod 29 = 27; Mallory computes A^m to get the same value. Bob never saw Alice's real half-key, so he cannot share this key with her.
concept: In DH MitM, each victim shares a key with the attacker.

subject: Networking
stem: A student script computes the parallel trust of 0.72 and 0.10 as 0.72 + 0.10 = 0.82. What is wrong?
option_1: It should take only the larger of the two values, giving 0.72
option_2: It should multiply the two values: 0.72 x 0.10 = 0.072
option_3: It omits the overlap term: 0.72 + 0.10 - 0.072 = 0.748
option_4: Nothing is wrong; parallel trust is simply the plain sum
answer_text: It omits the overlap term: 0.72 + 0.10 - 0.072 = 0.748
explanation: The OR formula subtracts the probability that both succeed, otherwise sums can exceed 1. Multiplying gives the series (AND) result, which applies to sequential hops.
concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B).

subject: Networking
stem: Design the key exchange for the chat app so that neither passive nor active relays can read messages. Which design is sound?
option_1: RSA in which the server sends its public key unsigned and the client trusts and uses it at once to wrap a session key
option_2: Ephemeral DH (or ECDHE) over a large standard group, each half-key signed by a certificate-backed key, then a KDF
option_3: Static DH with p = 19, sending the resulting shared key in clear once so both ends can confirm they agree on it
option_4: Hard-code one RC4 key into both clients and skip key exchange, so no relay ever sees any key material on the wire
answer_text: Ephemeral DH (or ECDHE) over a large standard group, each half-key signed by a certificate-backed key, then a KDF
explanation: Ephemeral DH gives forward secrecy, signatures bind half-keys to identities, and a KDF produces proper session keys. A hard-coded key is shared by every installation and cannot be changed once it leaks.
concept: Authenticated ephemeral DH + KDF.

subject: Networking
stem: What are the two sublayers of the data link layer?
option_1: ARP and RARP
option_2: Logical Link Control (LLC) and Media Access Control (MAC)
option_3: Media Access Control (MAC) and Internet Protocol (IP)
option_4: Logical Link Control (LLC) and Physical Coding (PHY)
answer_text: Logical Link Control (LLC) and Media Access Control (MAC)
explanation: LLC is the upper sublayer that interfaces with the network layer; MAC is the lower sublayer that handles hardware addressing and medium access. PHY coding belongs to the physical layer, and ARP is a helper protocol, not a sublayer.
concept: Data link = LLC (upper) + MAC (lower).

subject: Networking
stem: How are ARP requests and replies delivered?
option_1: Request by broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF); reply by unicast to the requester
option_2: Both by broadcast
option_3: Request by unicast to the gateway; reply by broadcast
option_4: Request by multicast; reply by broadcast
answer_text: Request by broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF); reply by unicast to the requester
explanation: The asker does not know the target MAC, so it broadcasts; only the owner of the IP answers, directly to the asker's MAC. 'Multicast request, broadcast reply' is a known slide error that the notes correct.
concept: ARP: who-has = broadcast; is-at = unicast.

subject: Networking
stem: What can an application gateway do that packet filters cannot?
option_1: Filter by source IP address
option_2: Drop packets with the SYN flag set
option_3: Make decisions on application data, such as authenticating users before relaying their sessions
option_4: Filter on destination port numbers
answer_text: Make decisions on application data, such as authenticating users before relaying their sessions
explanation: A proxy terminates the application session, so it can check usernames, commands or URLs. Port, flag and address filtering are standard packet-filter abilities.
concept: Application gateways decide on Layer 7 data.

subject: Networking
stem: What is the minimum RSA modulus size generally recommended today?
option_1: 2,048 bits
option_2: 1,024 bits
option_3: 128 bits
option_4: 512 bits
answer_text: 2,048 bits
explanation: 2,048-bit moduli are the common minimum, with 3,072-4,096 bits for long-lived or high-value keys. 512-bit keys have been factored and 1,024 bits is considered too weak.
concept: RSA >= 2,048 bits.

subject: Networking
stem: Traffic to a permitted web server on TCP 443 carries SQL injection in POST bodies. Why can a classic Layer 3/4 firewall not stop it?
option_1: Layer 3/4 firewalls cannot see port numbers
option_2: SQL injection uses UDP, which firewalls do not filter
option_3: SQL injection spoofs the source MAC address
option_4: It decides on addresses, ports and flags only, so it cannot inspect application payload logic
answer_text: It decides on addresses, ports and flags only, so it cannot inspect application payload logic
explanation: The packets are legitimate at Layers 3 and 4 (right address, right port), so a header-based filter passes them; only a WAF or deep inspection that understands HTTP can see the malicious payload. Saying such firewalls cannot see ports is false: ports are exactly what they filter on.
concept: Application-layer attacks need application-aware defences (WAF, DPI).

subject: Networking
stem: A client sends FIN with Seq = 4,000 and Ack = 7,000. What acknowledgement number does the server's ACK carry?
explanation: FIN consumes one sequence number, so the server acknowledges 4,000 + 1 = 4,001. 7,001 confuses the server's own sequence space with the client's.
concept: FIN consumes 1 sequence number.

subject: Networking
stem: A DHCP server sits behind a router with a relay agent. Why can it not stop starvation by limiting leases per source MAC in the Ethernet header?
option_1: Every relayed request arrives with the router's MAC as the frame source; the server must check CHADDR in the DHCP payload instead
option_2: Limiting MACs is forbidden by the DHCP standard
option_3: Relay agents encrypt the Ethernet header
option_4: DHCP requests carry no MAC address at all
answer_text: Every relayed request arrives with the router's MAC as the frame source; the server must check CHADDR in the DHCP payload instead
explanation: Layer 2 source addresses are rewritten at each hop, so the server only sees the router; the client's hardware address travels inside the DHCP message (CHADDR). DHCP messages do carry the client MAC, just not in the outer frame.
concept: Across routers, judge the DHCP payload (CHADDR), not the frame header.

subject: Networking
